claims.text: The initial HEA coating has a solid-solution-strengthened microstructure.
The initial coating has no pre-existing oxide layer at 25°C.
Wear resistance initially improves as ambient temperature increases.
The initial improvement in wear resistance persists only up to a critical temperature threshold.
Thermally activated solid-solution strengthening contributes to improved wear resistance at intermediate temperatures.
A protective oxide tribofilm forms as temperature rises and reduces friction and wear.
The protective tribofilm may contain Cr2O3 or Al2O3.
Wear at lower temperatures is dominated by abrasive mechanisms.
Increasing temperature thermally activates dislocation cross-slip.
Thermally activated dislocation cross-slip enhances solid-solution strengthening.
At approximately 0.4–0.5 times the coating melting temperature, the bulk matrix undergoes significant thermal softening.
Above the critical temperature, the oxide film may become unstable or spall.
Thermal softening and oxide-film failure cause a transition to severe adhesive wear.
The wear rate decreases between 25°C and approximately 400–500°C.
The wear rate increases sharply above approximately 500–600°C.
The performance-degradation boundary occurs above 0.5 times the melting temperature of the HEA coating.
Above the degradation boundary, thermal softening dominates the protective effect of surface oxidation.

contradictions.description: The tests may be performed in inert Argon, while protective oxide formation is presented as a central mediator without an atmosphere-dependent qualification. An inert atmosphere could suppress the proposed oxide pathway, so the mechanism is not consistently specified across the allowed atmospheres.
